source: Bosse, Muhlbacher, Wildman, Phillips, Schwarz (2026) Automating Forecasting Question Generation and Resolution for AI Evaluation (full text, section 5.5 and appendix A.19)
finding: The only recent test of subquestion decomposition for an LLM forecaster. Gemini 3 Pro forecasts got a little better, but the decomposed arm also got much more research and a different pipeline, so it is not a clean test of decomposition. Sub-forecasts were made blind to the parent question.
numbers: 500 questions sampled from 1,499. Agent writes subquestions (prompt says 1 to 5; text says 3 to 5). GPT-5 researches and forecasts each subquestion. Sub-forecasts plus their research are added to the context, then Gemini 3 Pro makes the final forecast. Brier 0.141 (95% CI 0.122-0.161) to 0.132 (CI 0.115-0.149). Better in 94.4% of 10,000 bootstrap samples. Sub-research was run 2 days after the baseline research (Oct 23 vs Oct 21 2025, some retries Oct 27).
quote: they don't know the top-level question
limits: No equal-token control (extra research agents and calls). CI of the paired difference not reported, only the two overlapping CIs. One final model, one question set, base rate 29.2%. Workshop paper (ICLR 2026 workshop). Later sub-research may have seen newer information.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open: this result bundles decomposition with extra retrieval. Test O3 against an arm given the same extra research budget without subquestion structure.

source: Bosse et al. (2026), Table 2 and abstract page, re-read to settle the 0.179 label and the calibration split
finding: The 0.179 label is settled: the abstract page gives Gemini 3 Pro 0.134, GPT-5 0.149, Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.179. The text extraction of Table 2 shifts the row labels, so they cannot be trusted. The decomposition gain was in calibration, not in discrimination.
numbers: Five full-set Brier values in order: 0.134 [0.123,0.146], 0.149 [0.141,0.157], 0.155 [0.146,0.163], 0.165 [0.155,0.176], 0.179 [0.168,0.191]. Subset: with subquestions Brier 0.132, calibration term 0.008, refinement 0.083. Baseline Brier 0.141, calibration term 0.026, refinement 0.091. So the calibration error fell 0.018 while refinement fell 0.008.
limits: Which of GPT-5 Mini or Gemini 2.5 Pro holds 0.155 and 0.165 is not settled by the extracted text. The calibration and refinement figures come from a garbled table; the arithmetic (0.018 minus 0.008 is about the 0.009 Brier gain) supports the reading. Base rate 29.2%, models predict YES too often (mean forecast 0.37 to 0.42).
agent_relevance: Closes the label question: 0.179 is Gemini 2.5 Flash. Suggests decomposition acts as a calibration correction (less overconfident forecasts) rather than as better ranking, so an O3 gate should be judged on calibration.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Bastos, Tetlock (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities (full text, Study 1 tables 4 and 5)
finding: Prompt-only Fermi, event and time decomposition did not move Brier for four 2024 LLMs on ForecastBench questions. Only base-rate prompts helped; a Bayesian-style prompt hurt.
numbers: Study 1: 38 prompts, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B; control Brier 0.208 to 0.227 by model. Mixed-model difference from control (positive = worse): Fermi Estimate +0.008 (BH-adjusted p .774), Event Decomposition +0.007 (.774), Time Decomposition -0.008 (.774). Preregistered t-tests: Fermi +0.004 (N 389, adj p .767), Event +0.002 (N 391, adj .818), Time -0.013 (N 385, unadjusted p .096, adj .210). Significant after adjustment: Frequency-Based Reasoning, Base Rate First, Step-Back (better); Bayesian Reasoning (+0.030, p<.001) and Propose-Evaluate-Select (worse).
limits: No retrieval: the model forecasts from its own knowledge, so Brier sits near 0.21 (0.25 is always-0.5). Decomposition has little evidence to work on. Study 2 added o1 and o1-mini with 4000 output tokens; its decomposition rows were not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Gap 1, no-retrieval half: decomposition by prompt alone is neutral for a model with no tools. Do not count a decomposition prompt as a free gain.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models (section 5 retrieval, section 7 ablations, appendix F prompts)
finding: The sub-question step lives inside the search-query generator and is never removed. One query prompt says 'write down sub-questions' first, and the system combines it with a plain query prompt. Only fine-tuning and retrieval are ablated.
numbers: Ablations (test Brier): full system 0.179; GPT-3.5 fine-tuned in place of GPT-4 0.182; no fine-tuning 0.186 (+0.007); no fine-tuning and no retrieval 0.206 (best baseline model 0.208; crowd 0.146).
quote: Start off by writing down sub-questions. Then use your sub-questions to help steer the search queries
limits: No ablation isolates sub-question queries. Retrieval plus fine-tuning together are worth about 0.027 Brier, so the sub-question share is bounded by that and is probably smaller. Search cost per question is not reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open (no ablation exists). Bound: the whole retrieval stack is worth about 0.02 Brier. Cheap to test ourselves: the same query prompt with and without the sub-question line.

source: Paleka, Goel, Geiping, Tramer (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters (Table 2, section 5)
finding: Violations of the Cond check track forecasting error across forecasters, but a patching method built on consistency checks did not improve Brier. Consistency is a diagnostic of a model, not yet a per-question gate that adds accuracy.
numbers: Correlation of consistency violation with Brier (arbitrage / frequentist): Cond scraped 0.92 / 0.87, NewsAPI 0.71 / 0.69. CondCond 0.78 / 0.71 and 0.75 / 0.69. And 0.68 / 0.72 and 0.54 / 0.71. Aggregated 0.62 / 0.85 and 0.49 / 0.66. Some checks are near zero or negative (Negation NewsAPI -0.36 / -0.13, Or -0.24 / -0.31, ExpEvidence -0.11 / 0.06). ArbitrageForecaster raised consistency only on the checks it was built on, did not carry over to held-out checks, and 'does not reliably' improve ground-truth Brier.
limits: Correlations are across a small set of forecaster configurations, not across questions, so they do not show a per-question gate works. Only a few of 10 checks are strong on both datasets. Cond is a decomposition-style check (P(A and B) = P(A) P(B given A)). No comparison against plain decomposition.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: no for patching; untested as a gate. Use the Cond gap as a monitor that flags an unreliable forecast and triggers more effort (resample, escalate), not as an automatic fix.

source: Radhakrishnan et al. (2023) Question Decomposition Improves the Faithfulness of Model-Generated Reasoning (Table 4 re-read together with the text)
finding: Gap 10 resolved. Chain of thought is slightly ahead of chain-of-thought decomposition, by 0.4 points on average. The 87.0 and 88.0 in the 'All Tasks' row of the extracted table are not those two methods; the averages are 86.0 and 85.6.
numbers: Text: CoT decomposition is 'only underperforming it by 0.4% (absolute) on average'. Column checks: zero-shot average 72.8 equals (77+82+71+61)/4; few-shot 79.7 equals (77+88+79+74.7)/4. CoT average 86.0, CoT decomposition 85.6, factored decomposition 81.8. HotpotQA: CoT 78.7, CoT decomposition 77.3, factored 83.0.
limits: The text extraction of Table 4 is scrambled across columns; the 0.4 gap in the prose and the two arithmetic checks settle it. K18 quotes HotpotQA factored 83.0 vs 87.3: 87.3 sits on the OpenBookQA row in the extract, so re-check that comparison before reuse.
agent_relevance: Decomposition inside one context buys no accuracy over plain CoT; its value is faithfulness. Correct a18, b11, c22 to CoT 86.0 vs CoT-decomposition 85.6.

source: Liu, Villarreal, Rahgouy, Das, Zhang, Ren, Feng (2025) LLM for Complex Reasoning Task: An Exploratory Study in Fermi Problems
finding: On Kalyan's real Fermi set, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 Turbo and Llama 3 70B all stayed under 0.5 fp_score even with detailed prompts, except GPT-4 at exactly 0.500 at the top prompt level. Standard (clear, concise) questions scored higher than specific ones.
numbers: 556 test questions (252 standard, 304 specific). GPT-4: 0.466 / 0.479 / 0.500 across the prompt levels shown; Llama 3.0: 0.439 / 0.469 / 0.460. GPT-4 level 0 on standard questions 0.511. GPT-3.5 level 0 0.442.
limits: Models are 2023-2024 era; no reasoning model, no tools. Prompts follow the TELeR taxonomy, not forced decomposition. No 2025-2026 frontier model on this set was found; the web search quota ran out during this session, so a gap in coverage is likely.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open for frontier models. Best published fp_score found is still 0.50 (GPT-4 Turbo). Plan: run our own agent on the Kalyan test set as an O3 benchmark.

source: Epstein, Winnicki, Sornwanee, Dwaraknath (2025) LLMs are Overconfident: Evaluating Confidence Interval Calibration with FermiEval
finding: LLM intervals on Fermi questions are too narrow and coverage stays flat as the requested level rises. The paper theorises that self-generated reasoning traces narrow the answer distribution, but it does not test decomposition prompts.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini observed coverage: 0.63 at nominal 0.90, 0.59 at 0.95, 0.64 at 0.99. Log-probability method: 0.85, 0.89, 0.90. Across models nominal 99% intervals cover about 65%. Conformal adjustment gives near-nominal coverage; Winkler score falls 54% (reductions 25.2% at p=0.90, 27.8% at 0.95, 59.4% at 0.99).
limits: Appendix G 'Tunnel Vision' is a stated hypothesis with no measurement: low-entropy decoding inflates confidence and multi-sample decoding should restore calibration. Questions are Fermi style with order-of-magnitude answers.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: no study found that compares decomposed against direct LLM intervals. The evidence points to resampling plus conformal-style widening as the fix. Widen intervals by a measured factor rather than trust stated levels.

source: MacGregor and Armstrong (1994) Judgmental Decomposition: When Does It Work? (conditions text and not-extreme results, re-read)
finding: The authors state three conditions for decomposition to work: the target is hard to estimate, part errors are smaller than whole errors, and part errors are not strongly positively correlated. They show a failure case where the parts were no easier and not independent.
numbers: Not extreme problems: decomposition raised median error 458% (p<0.05, two-tailed; authors note the test overstates significance because estimates are not independent). Compounding example 1.2 x 1.2 = 1.44. Argentine immigrants: interquartile range 2.14 decomposed vs 1.00 global, although each part had the same range as the whole.
limits: 1994 student estimation tasks, six problems. Authors say the conditions 'are not easy to specify in operational terms'. No test of re-estimation or averaging to cut correlated error.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 5: a gate should check the three conditions per question. Condition 2 can be probed by asking for confidence per part and for the whole; condition 3 by checking whether the parts share an anchor or source.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments (Judgment and Decision Making 11(5))
finding: Gap 3 evidence: training worked, but decomposition or Fermi-izing was not a labelled component and was not tested alone. The reader summary of the page says neither term appears in the paper.
numbers: Randomized training vs control over 4 tournament years. Brier improvement over control: year 1 probability training 10%, scenario training 11%; year 2 12%; year 3 6%; year 4 7%. Ns control/training: 152/232, 194/205, 116/97, 131/102. Training under one hour. Self-reported comparison classes related to better accuracy (p<.001); post-mortem and other-perspectives related to worse (reverse causation likely). Training effect partly mediated by forecasts per question in 3 of 4 years.
limits: Opened as a fetched, summarised page, not the PDF. Bundle of principles (CHAMPS KNOW); authors warn they may interact. Closest item is year-1 scenario training that included identifying key causal drivers. No arm tests decomposition alone.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 closed negatively: the strongest causal training study gives no effect size for Fermi-izing. O3 rests on the estimation literature (MA94, Barrera-Lemarchand 2026), not on superforecaster training evidence.

source: Hauenstein, Thomas, Illingworth, Dougherty (2025) Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting (Psychological Science)
finding: A re-analysis of the Mellers et al. (2014) tournament data with an item response model found the team and training effects shrink, vanish or flip once extraneous variables are controlled. Abstract only; full text not opened.
numbers: First 2 tournament years; best-fit models included extraneous variables that 'substantially eliminated, reduced, and, in some cases, even reversed' the effects of teaming and training on latent ability. Exact effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC record). It concerns training and teaming in general, not decomposition. It weakens how much any one training ingredient can be credited.
agent_relevance: Treat superforecaster-training claims as weak support for any single technique. Do not cite Mellers 2014 for decomposition.

source: Barrera-Lemarchand, Lescano-Charreau, Ruiz, Caceres, Carrillo, Sigman, Navajas (2026) Collective problem decomposition improves the wisdom of deliberative crowds, Nature Communications 17
finding: The best causal human test found of instructed Fermi decomposition versus combining guesses. The effect is real but small, and solo use of the method helped less than group use.
numbers: Study 1 (500 people, 125 groups of 4, 8 general-knowledge estimation questions): consensus error 0.72 vs 1.18 for the mean of members' initial guesses (paired d=0.81). Study 2 (preregistered, 240 people, 60 groups): instructed to decompose vs instructed to share and combine numbers; lower error with decomposition, Mann-Whitney z=2.1, p=0.039, Cohen's d=0.26, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.61. Study 3 (160 people, 20 groups vs 80 solo): participants after group Fermi had lower individual error than after solo Fermi, beta=-0.24 (95% CI -0.38 to -0.10), d=0.26.
limits: Study 2 CI includes zero. General-knowledge items, online chat. Does not isolate decomposition from deliberation. Solo decomposition (closest to one LLM) was the weaker arm.
agent_relevance: Supports O3 modestly: forced decomposition beats number-averaging by about a quarter of a standard deviation. The solo-vs-group gap suggests several independent decompositions merged by reasoning could beat one.

source: Deliberation in Guesstimation (Cognitive Science, 2025; think-aloud study and two-response paradigm)
finding: People asked for a full distribution on guesstimation questions stay overconfident even after deliberating. Deliberation raised answer quality over the gut-feeling answer.
numbers: Experiment 2 calibration: where 10% of z-scores should fall below a point, 42% did; where 90% should, only 68% did. Deliberated answers significantly better than gut answers (Experiment 1).
limits: Author list and sample sizes not extracted (read from the Europe PMC full text; title and journal are the safe label). Deliberation is not purely decomposition: participants also used analogies and replaced the question.
agent_relevance: Gap 7, human side: decomposition-style deliberation does not remove overconfidence, so the agent should widen intervals by a measured factor after decomposing.

source: Prasad, Koller, Hartmann, Clark, Sabharwal, Bansal, Khot (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models
finding: A concrete trigger for decomposing: decompose only when the executor fails on the task, recursively. This beat always-decompose (plan-and-execute) and never-decompose (ReAct). Always-decompose hurt on WebShop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 executor, success rate (%): ALFWorld ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, ADaPT 71.6 (max depth 3). WebShop ReAct 32.0, Plan-and-Execute 17.0, ADaPT 44.0. TextCraft ReAct 19.0, Plan-and-Execute 27.0, ADaPT 52.0 (max depth 4). Headline gains up to 28.3, 27 and 33 points.
limits: Agentic text environments with a checkable success signal, not forecasting. In forecasting there is no immediate success signal, so a proxy is needed.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the first tested trigger is 'try directly, decompose on failure'. For forecasting, replace failure with a proxy such as the spread of 3 to 5 direct answers. Not yet tested.

source: Sprague, Yin, Rodriguez, Jiang, Wadhwa, Singhal, Zhao, Ye, Mahowald, Durrett (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning (ICLR 2025)
finding: Across more than 100 papers and 20 datasets on 14 models, explicit stepwise reasoning pays mainly on math, symbolic and logic tasks. Elsewhere the gain is tiny and may vanish at matched compute.
numbers: Mean CoT gain over direct: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logic 6.9 points. Top three categories: 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. Other categories: 56.8 vs 56.1. On MMLU the gain appears mostly when the question or response contains an equals sign.
quote: a truly fair comparison between the methods should match the compute of the two methods
limits: About chain of thought in general, not decomposition of forecast questions. 2024 models, before most reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a cheap trigger is whether the question has a numeric, multiplicative structure. Not a forecasting test. Warns that equal-compute baselines are needed (links gap 1).

source: Dhuliawala, Komeili, Xu, Raileanu, Li, Celikyilmaz, Weston (2023) Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models
finding: Answering follow-up questions in separate contexts, blind to the first draft, did better than answering them with the draft in view. Closest LLM evidence on whether sub-answers should be blind to the parent.
numbers: Longform biographies, Llama 65B, FACTSCORE: few-shot 55.9; CoVe joint 60.8; factored 63.7; factor+revise 71.4. MultiSpanQA F1: joint 0.46, factored 0.48. List tasks: two-step best on Wikidata, factored best on Wiki-Category.
limits: Factual verification of generated text, not probability forecasting. Llama 65B. Gain of factored over joint is 2.9 points. Compute differs between variants.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly answered: blindness helps by stopping the model copying its first answer; supports Bosse's blind design. Not tested for numeric forecasts.

source: Wang, Wei, Schuurmans, Le, Chi, Narang, Chowdhery, Zhou (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (ICLR 2023)
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the majority answer lifts accuracy a lot on arithmetic and less on soft tasks. It is the closest tested LLM mechanism for averaging out independent errors, which MA94 says decomposition needs.
numbers: Gains over greedy CoT: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 (points).
limits: Majority vote over final answers, not part-level re-estimation. Errors from one model are correlated through shared beliefs, so averaging helps less than if they were independent. No test with decomposed parts.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 only indirectly: re-sample each part and the whole, then take the median. The gain for correlated part errors is unmeasured.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting (ensemble results)
finding: Ensembling samples helps a tool-using agent but not a plain model, which fits the idea that averaging helps only when outputs are individually calibrated.
numbers: 201 questions. ReAct agent ensemble Brier 0.169 vs single agent 0.180 (human median 0.172; accuracy 73.9% vs 73.8%). Base LM GPT-4o ensemble 0.218 vs single 0.210 (worse). Base-LM ensemble sd 0.150; ReAct ensemble sd 0.092.
limits: Small set; ensemble sizes 3 to 4. No decomposition arm.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 indirect: use sampling only if the sampled forecasts are individually calibrated; otherwise averaging can hurt.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters; Bench to the Future (FutureSearch, 2025)
finding: Two 2025 forecasting evaluations of frontier models were keyword-scanned for a decomposition or sub-question ablation and contain none. They describe prompt or snapshot design (reference class first, multiple base rates) without testing it.
numbers: Lu: 464 Metaculus questions; frontier models' Brier ostensibly beats the crowd but stays significantly worse than top forecasters. Bench to the Future: about 20,000 crawled pages per question in the hermetic snapshot, built by exploring multiple base rates.
limits: Absence of evidence only, from a keyword search of the full text. Only abstract-level numbers were taken from these papers.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 6 remain unresolved in the literature this session could reach; a decomposition-vs-equal-compute test must be run by us.
